chapter.name: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
chapter.blurb: The concluding chapter of the Grade 8 Curiosity textbook, bringing together the year's learning to ask why Earth, among the planets, is a unique planet that supports life. Covers the thin life-supporting crust, the solar system's planets and the greenhouse effect, Earth's position, size and magnetic field, the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere that sustain life, asexual and sexual reproduction that keeps life continuing, and the triple planetary crisis of climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution that now threatens this balance.

scope_in.item: Earth is the only known planet, among perhaps billions, where life exists and thrives in all its forms

All life on Earth exists only in a very thin surface layer, the crust, which is tiny compared to the size of the whole planet; if Earth were the size of an apple, the crust would be as thin as the apple's skin (Fig. 13.1)
Earth's internal layers named in Figure 13.1: crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core, inner core

Two example 'interesting features of Earth' given in Table 13.1: air does not fly off into space (linked to Chapter 7's particles of a gas), and we can stand on the ground held by gravity while the heart pumps blood up to the head (linked to Chapter 5)
The eight planets of the solar system, in order of increasing distance from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, orbiting in nearly circular orbits
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are relatively small, rocky planets; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are large planets mostly made of gases

Data given in Table 13.2: Mercury (170 degrees Celsius, no atmosphere), Venus (450 degrees Celsius, radius 0.95 times Earth's, has an atmosphere), Earth (15 degrees Celsius, radius taken as 1, has an atmosphere)
General pattern that planets closer to the Sun are usually hotter, with Venus as the exception: it is hotter than Mercury even though farther from the Sun

The greenhouse effect: gases like carbon dioxide in a planet's atmosphere trap heat by absorbing radiation given off by the planet after the Sun warms it; Venus's carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere makes it the hottest planet, and Earth's much milder greenhouse effect keeps its temperature just right
The difference between the planetary greenhouse effect (gases trapping radiated heat) and a plant greenhouse (a closed, usually glass, space trapping warmed air)
Earth's distance from the Sun is just right for water to remain liquid; too close and water would evaporate, too far and it would freeze
The habitable zone (Goldilocks zone): the range of distances from a star over which water remains liquid
Earth is called the Blue Planet because most of its surface is covered with water, giving it a blue appearance from space
Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone; it may once have had liquid water, but no proof of life has been found there
Earth's nearly circular orbit keeps sunlight and heat nearly steady through the year, preventing extreme summers and winters

Earth is the right size to hold on to an atmosphere by gravity: a much smaller Earth (same density) would have gravity too weak to hold its gases, which would escape into space; Mars's atmosphere is 100 times thinner than Earth's and Mercury has none at all
A much larger Earth would have gravity strong enough to crush living things
The ozone layer, formed from oxygen, blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun that can damage living cells
India's Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission), launched in 2013 by ISRO, studied Mars's atmosphere, surface and signs of past water
Earth behaves like a giant magnet; its magnetic field is believed to originate from the movement of molten iron in Earth's core

Cosmic rays (from across the universe) and the solar wind (from the Sun) are harmful high-energy particles that can damage the atmosphere and reduce the ozone layer; Earth's magnetic field shields the planet by pushing many of these particles away
The atmosphere provides oxygen for respiration; in photosynthesis, plants use carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil, in sunlight, to make food and release oxygen
The mild greenhouse effect keeps Earth's temperature just high enough for liquid water; without an atmosphere Earth would lose heat to space and become too cold
The hydrosphere: all of Earth's water, in ponds, lakes, rivers, springs, seas, oceans and groundwater, covering about 70 per cent of Earth's surface
Water is a good solvent, transports nutrients from soil to leaves in plants, and in animals regulates body temperature, aids digestion and ensures hydration
Water vapour forms clouds and brings rain or snow, refilling rivers, lakes and groundwater; rainfall affects which plants and animals can live in a place

The geosphere: the solid parts of Earth -- rocks, soil and minerals -- which supply nutrient-rich soil (from broken-down rock and remains of plants and animals) and minerals like salt, coal, oil, iron and copper
Geodiversity: the variety of landforms, rocks and soils on Earth and the processes that shape and alter them, helping create unique habitats
The biosphere: all living beings together with the places where they live (land, water, air)
Plants make food by photosynthesis, animals eat plants or other animals, and decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil

Earth's balance: the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere support and affect one another, so even a small change, like cutting down a forest, can impact rainfall, soil, air quality and animals
Reproduction ensures the continuity of life; genes, the genetic material/instructions stored in every cell, are passed from parent to offspring, for example so that a calf grows into a cow
Reproduction can also pass on small changes across generations that help organisms adapt, such as camels developing humps for deserts, or some bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics
Asexual reproduction: a single parent produces new individuals that are exact copies of itself (in terms of genetic instructions)
Vegetative propagation: a new plant grows from a planted leaf, stem or root, as with ginger, a sprouted potato's 'eyes', or a money plant cutting
Other examples of asexual reproduction: bacteria and amoeba dividing into two identical individuals; Hydra budding; Planaria regrowing from a body fragment

Sexual reproduction: two parents (usually male and female) are involved; this occurs in animals, flowering plants (which have male and female parts) and some microorganisms like bacteria and yeast (which have two mating types)
Gametes are specialised reproductive cells carrying half a parent's genetic material; male and female gametes join to form a new cell with a complete, mixed set of instructions
Sexual reproduction produces variation because each gamete carries a different mix of instructions, so offspring resemble but are not identical to either parent

Sexual reproduction in plants: pollen (male gametes, in the anther) and ovules (female gametes); pollination transfers pollen; fertilisation forms a zygote that becomes the seed; the flesh around the ovule becomes the fruit; example of seed dispersal by a bird eating fruit and excreting the seed elsewhere

Sexual reproduction in animals: gametes are sperm (male) and eggs (female); external fertilisation in water for fish and frogs (zygote/embryo develop in water); internal fertilisation for birds and mammals

In birds, the fertilised egg (zygote) is laid, and the embryo develops during hatching, using food stored in the egg; in most mammals, the embryo develops inside the mother's body, nourished by her until birth
Life on Earth depends on a delicate balance of living and non-living things; small changes in global temperature, oxygen levels or the ozone layer can endanger life
The triple planetary crisis: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution

Climate change: burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane) that trap heat and cause global warming, which can melt ice caps, raise sea levels and flood coastal cities, cause extreme weather, and lead to species loss; this extra carbon is released faster than trees, plants and ocean plankton can absorb it

Biodiversity loss: destroying habitats makes plants and animals disappear and upsets ecosystems, for example if grasses vanish, herbivores like deer or grasshoppers struggle, and predators like tigers or foxes then lose their food too

Pollution: air pollution from factories, vehicles and burning fuels causes breathing problems, damages crops, and leads to smog and acid rain; water and soil pollution from factory, farm and plastic waste and poor waste disposal harm aquatic life, reduce crop yield and spread harmful substances through the food chain

International agreements: the Montreal Protocol (1987, reduced CFCs to help the ozone layer recover), the Earth Summit (1992, international efforts on climate and biodiversity), the Kyoto Protocol (2005) and the Paris Agreement (2015), both committing countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions; the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting warming to below 1.5 degrees Celsius, and that as of 2025 the world is not on track to meet it

Ways to protect the balance: cutting greenhouse gases with renewable energy (solar, wind), improving energy use, environmentally friendly travel, preserving biodiversity, sustainable use of resources, and everyday actions like reusing, repairing, recycling, and saving energy and water

concepts.name: Earth's thin, life-supporting crust
concepts.description: Earth is the only known planet where life exists and thrives, and all of that life is confined to a very thin outer layer called the crust.
concepts.idea: Compared to the size of the planet, all life on Earth exists only in an extremely thin surface layer, the crust.
concepts.rule: We have reached the final chapter of the book, where we put together everything learnt so far to understand why Earth is unlike any other place in the known universe. Earth is a planet orbiting the Sun, but it is not just any planet: among perhaps billions of planets in the universe, it is the only one known where life exists and thrives in all its forms. All the mountains, rivers, forests, animals and people are found on just a very thin layer on the surface of the planet, called the crust. From the tallest mountain to the deepest ocean trench, this life-supporting crust is tiny compared to the size of the whole Earth. If Earth were the size of an apple, the crust would be as thin as the apple's skin. Earth's other internal layers, shown in Figure 13.1, are the upper mantle, the lower mantle, the outer core and the inner core.
concepts.example: If Earth were shrunk down to the size of an apple, its crust, where all life exists, would be as thin as the apple's skin.

concepts.name: Planets of the solar system and the greenhouse effect
concepts.description: The eight planets of the solar system in order from the Sun, the difference between rocky and gas planets, and why the greenhouse effect makes Venus hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
concepts.idea: The greenhouse effect happens when gases like carbon dioxide trap heat radiated from a warmed planet, which is why Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest planet in the solar system.
concepts.rule: Our solar system has eight planets that go around the Sun in nearly circular orbits. In order of increasing distance from the Sun, they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are relatively small, rocky planets, while Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are large planets made mostly of gases. All planets get their energy from the Sun, so planets closer to the Sun are generally hotter and planets farther away are generally colder. However, Venus, the second planet from the Sun, is the hottest planet in the solar system, even hotter than Mercury which is closer to the Sun. This is because Venus's atmosphere is almost entirely carbon dioxide gas, which does not let heat escape; this is called the greenhouse effect. On Earth too, gases like carbon dioxide in the atmosphere trap heat by absorbing the radiation given off by Earth after it is warmed by the Sun, and this greenhouse effect plays an important role in keeping just the right temperature on Earth. This planetary greenhouse effect is different from a plant greenhouse used to grow plants in a cool climate: a plant greenhouse simply traps warmed air because it is a closed space, usually with glass walls, while the greenhouse effect on a planet works by gases absorbing radiation.
concepts.example: Venus has an average temperature of 450 degrees Celsius, hotter than Mercury's 170 degrees Celsius, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun, because Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat through the greenhouse effect.

s: Same mechanism applies to Earth, more mildly

s: Reason using chapter's greenhouse effect ideas

concepts.name: Earth's position, size and magnetic field support life
concepts.description: Three factors that make Earth suitable for life: its position in the Sun's habitable (Goldilocks) zone that keeps water liquid, its size which gives it enough gravity to hold an atmosphere including the protective ozone layer, and its magnetic field which shields it from cosmic rays and the solar wind.
concepts.idea: Earth supports life because it is at the right distance from the Sun for liquid water, the right size to hold on to a protective atmosphere, and has a magnetic field that shields it from harmful particles from space.
concepts.rule: The most important reason Earth can support life is its distance from the Sun: it is just at the right distance for temperatures that allow water to exist in liquid form. If Earth were closer to the Sun, all the water would evaporate; if it were farther away, all the water would freeze. The range of distances from a star over which water remains liquid is called the habitable zone, or the Goldilocks zone. Because most of Earth's surface is covered in water, Earth looks blue from space and is called the Blue Planet. Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone; scientists think Mars may once have had liquid water, though no proof of life has been found there yet. Earth's size also matters. Earth's nearly circular orbit keeps the amount of sunlight and heat it receives nearly steady through the year, preventing extreme summers and winters. Earth is also the right size to hold on to an atmosphere: Earth's gravity pulls objects, including gas particles, towards it, and if Earth were much smaller (with the same density) its gravity would be too weak to hold the gases of the atmosphere, which would escape into space. Mars, which is smaller than Earth, has an atmosphere 100 times thinner than Earth's, and Mercury has no atmosphere at all. If Earth were too large, its stronger gravity could crush living things. Because Earth can hold an atmosphere, it also has an ozone layer, formed from oxygen, which blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun that can damage living cells. Finally, Earth behaves like a giant magnet, and it is believed that the movement of molten iron in Earth's core may be the origin of Earth's magnetic field. Earth is constantly hit by high-energy particles: cosmic rays that come from across the universe, and the solar wind that comes from the Sun. These particles can damage the atmosphere and reduce the ozone layer, letting in more harmful ultraviolet rays. Earth's magnetic field acts like a protective shield, pushing many of these harmful particles away and keeping the atmosphere, and life, safe.
concepts.example: Mars has an atmosphere 100 times thinner than Earth's, and Mercury has none at all, because both are too small for their gravity to hold on to an atmosphere the way Earth's gravity does.

concepts.name: Earth's interacting systems: air, water, land and life
concepts.description: How the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere -- air and sunlight, water, soil and rocks, and living things -- interact, and why keeping them in balance is essential for sustaining life on Earth.
concepts.idea: Life on Earth is sustained by the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere working together, and even a small change in one can affect the others.
concepts.rule: The atmosphere contains oxygen, which humans, animals and plants use for respiration. In the presence of sunlight, plants take carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil to prepare food by photosynthesis, releasing oxygen in the process. The mild greenhouse effect keeps the temperature just high enough for water to remain liquid; without an atmosphere, Earth would lose heat to space and become too cold. Water is essential for life: it covers about 70 per cent of Earth's surface, found in ponds, lakes, rivers, springs, seas, oceans and groundwater, and all this water forms the hydrosphere. Water is a good solvent, transports nutrients from soil to leaves in plants, and in animals regulates body temperature, aids digestion and ensures hydration. Water vapour in the air forms clouds and brings rain or snow, refilling rivers, lakes and groundwater, and rainfall affects the kinds of plants and animals that can live in a place. Beneath our feet lies the geosphere: the solid parts of Earth, including rocks, soil and minerals, which provide almost everything life needs, from soil that helps plants grow to minerals that give us salt, coal, oil and metals like iron and copper. Soil is rich in nutrients like nitrogen and potassium that come from the slow breakdown of rocks and the remains of plants and animals. Geodiversity is the variety of landforms, rocks and soils on Earth, along with the processes that shape and alter them, and it helps create unique habitats. All living beings, along with the places where they live, make up the biosphere, which includes land, water and air, where life interacts with its surroundings to survive and grow. Plants make food through photosynthesis, animals eat plants or other animals, and decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. Earth is like a vast, living system where land, air, water and living things support and affect one another; even a small change in one part, like cutting down a forest, can impact rainfall, soil, air quality and the animals that live there, so preserving this balance is essential for keeping Earth healthy.
concepts.example: Cutting down a forest can affect rainfall, soil quality, air quality and the animals living there, showing how Earth's systems are all connected.

concepts.name: Reproduction: asexual, sexual and genetic variation
concepts.description: How reproduction, guided by genes passed from parents to offspring, keeps each kind of living thing continuing; asexual reproduction makes exact copies from one parent, while sexual reproduction combines gametes from two parents to create variation.
concepts.idea: Genes carried in every cell pass instructions from parents to offspring; asexual reproduction copies these instructions exactly from one parent, while sexual reproduction mixes instructions from two parents, producing variation.
concepts.rule: If plants and animals did not reproduce, life would eventually disappear from Earth; reproduction ensures that each type of organism continues to exist. Parents pass on instructions to their offspring about how to develop from a single cell; these instructions, called genetic material or genes, are stored inside every cell of a living being, so a calf grows into a cow. Reproduction does more than create more of the same kind of living being: it also allows for small changes in the instructions passed down from parents to offspring, which can help a plant or animal survive better in a new environment, for example camels developing humps to store fat and survive in deserts, or some bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics. In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces new individuals that are exact copies of itself, in terms of the instructions inside the cell; vegetative propagation is one example, where a plant grows again when a leaf, stem or root is planted in soil, as with ginger, the 'eyes' of a sprouted potato, or a money plant cutting. Single-celled organisms like bacteria and amoeba also reproduce asexually by dividing into two identical individuals; Hydra grows buds that break off and grow into new individuals; and Planaria, a flatworm, can regrow from just a fragment of its body. In sexual reproduction, two parents are usually involved, called male and female; this happens in animals, in flowering plants (which have male and female parts), and even in some microorganisms like bacteria and yeast, which have two 'mating types'. Each parent makes specialised reproductive cells called gametes, which carry only half of the parent's genetic material; when male and female gametes join, they form a new cell with a complete set of instructions, half from each parent. Because each gamete carries a different set of instructions, offspring are not identical to either parent, which is why brothers and sisters can look different from each other. In plants, pollen grains inside the anther are the male gametes, and ovules deep inside the flower are the female gametes; pollination carries pollen to another flower, and fertilisation is when the male and female gametes combine, forming a zygote that becomes the seed, while the fleshy part around the ovule develops into a fruit. In animals, gametes are called sperm (male) and eggs (female); in fish and frogs, fertilisation happens outside the body in water, and the zygote develops into an embryo in water. In birds and mammals, sperm are deposited inside the female's body and fertilisation happens internally; in birds, the fertilised egg is laid, and the embryo develops during hatching using food stored in the egg, while in most mammals the embryo develops inside the mother's body, which supplies food and oxygen until the baby is born.
concepts.example: A baby may inherit a nose similar to the mother and eyes similar to the father because sexual reproduction mixes genetic instructions from both parents in different ways each time.

concepts.name: The triple planetary crisis and protecting Earth
concepts.description: Climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution -- together called the triple planetary crisis -- threaten the delicate balance that sustains life on Earth, and international agreements and everyday actions aim to protect it.
concepts.idea: Human activities are disturbing the delicate balance of Earth's systems through climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution, together called the triple planetary crisis, but international agreements and everyday actions can help protect this balance.
concepts.rule: Life on Earth depends on a delicate balance of living and non-living things working together, but human actions are disturbing this balance; even small changes in global temperature, oxygen levels or the ozone layer can put life at risk. Today, the biggest environmental challenges are climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution, together known as the triple planetary crisis. Burning fossil fuels like coal and oil releases greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane, which trap even more heat in the atmosphere and cause global warming; normally trees, plants and ocean plankton absorb carbon dioxide, but burning fossil fuels releases extra carbon that was locked underground for millions of years, faster than Earth can absorb it. Even a small increase in temperature can melt ice caps, raise sea levels which could flood coastal cities, cause extreme weather, and lead to plants and animals disappearing; these long-term changes are called climate change. When natural habitats are destroyed, plants and animals may disappear, upsetting ecosystems: for example, if grasses vanish, animals that feed on them like deer or grasshoppers struggle to survive, and without herbivores, predators like tigers or foxes lose their food too. Air pollution from factories, vehicles and burning fuels harms people and nature, causing breathing problems, damaging crops, and leading to smog and acid rain; water and soil pollution from factory, farm and plastic waste, and poor waste disposal, harm aquatic life, make water unsafe, reduce crop yield, and spread harmful substances through the food chain. Countries around the world have made global agreements to protect the environment: the Montreal Protocol (1987) helped reduce harmful chemicals called CFCs, allowing the ozone layer to slowly recover; the Earth Summit (1992) led to international efforts on climate change and biodiversity; the Kyoto Protocol (2005) and the Paris Agreement (2015) committed countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with the Paris Agreement setting a goal to limit global warming to below 1.5 degrees Celsius, though as of 2025 the world is not on track to meet that goal. Protecting the climate means cutting greenhouse gases by using renewable energy like solar and wind, improving energy use, and choosing environmentally friendly ways to travel; preserving biodiversity is also key, and local communities can help by using natural resources sustainably. Everyday actions like reusing, repairing and recycling, and saving energy and water, also add up and make a difference.

questions.q: Design a short awareness poster plan, naming the triple planetary crisis, one cause and one solution for each of its three parts, based on the chapter.
questions.a: For example: Climate change -- cause: burning fossil fuels; solution: use renewable energy like solar and wind. Biodiversity loss -- cause: destruction of natural habitats; solution: protect and preserve natural habitats and use resources sustainably. Pollution -- cause: factory, vehicle and waste pollution; solution: reduce, reuse and recycle, and manage waste responsibly. Any reasonable cause-solution pair for each of the three parts is acceptable.
